title: Year two close: the porch
hook: the school of the porch is yours to visit any time

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahead, to the big questions. Your line was the big questions. Did you write yours at the top of a blank page? Leave it there. Day six hundred ninety-six. The last day of year two.

A porch is a strange kind of room. It has a roof, so you can shelter there. It has no front wall, so the street comes right up to it. People stop on the steps to talk, to wait out the rain, to watch the evening come in. Nobody checks a ticket. You can stay an hour or a minute, and come back whenever you like. A school of philosophy started on exactly that kind of porch. We have spent a whole year sitting on it. Today we close year two.
screen: `A ROOF, BUT NO FRONT WALL.` → `NOBODY CHECKS A TICKET.` → `A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: First, what a porch asks of you. On day six hundred eighty-nine we stood in Athens at the painted porch where Zeno taught in the open. Notice what that means. Nobody enrolls on a porch. You step up from the street, and you can step down again. Second, how the Handbook sends you off. Near its end, in a passage we met on day three hundred eighty-five, Epictetus turns to his student and asks: how long will you put it off? You are not a boy any more. The contest is now; it can't be postponed. Then he points to Socrates, who became who he was by attending to reason in everything, and says: you are not yet a Socrates, but you can live as someone who wants to be one. The book doesn't end with a diploma. It ends by pointing at today. Third, not finished, and that's fine. Nobody leaves a year of reading as a sage. Epictetus asked his students to show him even one Stoic and implied he'd never seen one; Seneca said plainly that he wasn't wise. What the porch offers instead is a direction: wanting to be the kind of person Socrates was, and taking the next step on an ordinary day. Fourth, the porch stays open. A porch has no door to lock behind you. Whatever you kept from this year, a morning intention, an evening question, a delayed reply, you can step back up onto it any day you want. Tomorrow, year three: six questions.
screen: `NOBODY ENROLLS ON A PORCH.` · `HOW LONG WILL YOU PUT IT OFF?` · `NOT YET A SOCRATES.` · `A PORCH HAS NO DOOR TO LOCK.` · then, large: `THE PORCH STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Find a step, if you can: a porch, a stoop, a front step, a stair in your building. Or sit in a doorway, half in and half out. Sit down. Feel the roof or the sky above you, and the open side in front. Let the year come to you as one picture: whichever teacher, line or moment stayed. Don't sort it or grade it. Just sit with it, the way people sit on steps at the end of a day. The bell holds the time.
Year two close: the end of a year with the Stoics, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, on a porch with no door, open whenever you return. Today's word, and the last of year two.
Your line: the porch stays open. Choose one Stoic habit to carry into year three, and do it once more tonight. Then rest. Tomorrow, six questions. Day six hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some people who study the Stoics keep returning to a handful of texts, the Handbook, Seneca's letters and the Meditations, rereading them over the years as guides rather than rulebooks.

myth: the Stoics are named after a porch

near its end, the Handbook tells students to wait until they're ready
Epictetus says the contest is now and can't be put off.
Epictetus told his student he must already be a Socrates
not yet a Socrates, he says, but live as someone who wants to be one.

fork.setup: you're Epictetus's student, and the lessons are ending. you say: I'll start properly once I'm ready. what does he answer?
options: take all the time you need
how long will you put it off? the contest is now
fork.reveal: Handbook 51: you are no longer a boy; the contest is here and can't be postponed. live now as someone who wants to be a Socrates.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the Stoics.
what it means: the end of a year on the porch, which stays open to return to any day.

what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laertius 7.5 has Zeno teaching in the Stoa Poikile, and Handbook 51 ends the course with 'how long will you put it off?' and the call to live as one who wants to be a Socrates.

sources.work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: Year close: names the year's blocks (Handbook, Discourses, Seneca, Meditations, the wider porch) and points to year three, day 697 'Six questions'.
Diogenes Laertius 7.5: Zeno taught in the Stoa Poikile, and his followers were called Stoics after it. Date 'around 300 BCE' is approximate.

New teach: a porch asks no enrollment (brief callback to 689), Handbook 51 'how long will you put it off... not yet a Socrates' (callback to day 385), and 'not finished, and that's fine'. Meditations 12.36 (three acts) was avoided because day 636 built a day on it. Cut the hook's 'around three hundred years before the common era' and the trapdoor's 'about 300 BCE' (no cited text gives the date), and 'the way people have always sat on steps'. Original set to null.

Enchiridion 51 paraphrased: how long will you delay; you are no longer a youth; the contest is now and cannot be put off; Socrates became what he was by attending to nothing but reason; though not yet a Socrates, live as one who wishes to be one. Confirm.
